newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Future U.S. power haunts Singapore naval show.
newsitem.headline: Future U.S. power haunts Singapore naval show.

text.p: A major naval defence show takes place in Singapore this week at a time when military spending in the prosperous region is booming, fuelled partly by jitters over the U.S. defence umbrella in the area, analysts said.
About a dozen warships will dock in Singapore while defence companies from the U.S., Russia, Britain and France will be hawking their wares at the naval show IMDEX Asia 1997, which runs from May 6-9.

"It is anticipated that by the end of the century, maritime defence expenditure in the Asia-Pacific region may well outstrip that of Western Europe and even North America," Roger Marriott, the chairman of the show, told reporters.
"Countries here are taking a peek over their shoulders and are wondering if the U.S. will maintain their large naval presence in the area," one defence official said.
The U.S. has previously said it would maintain a force of 100,000 soldiers in Asia, concentrated mostly in Japan and South Korea, and that it had no plans to withdraw from the region.
Marriott estimated that nations in the region will spend US$111-$127 billion in naval procurement alone from now until the 2010-2015 period.

"We haven't even discussed Japan or China," he said. "I just believe that every nation is aware of their responsiblity in the maintenance of their security, their exclusive economic zones, of fighting piracy."

The increased spending is being spurred by the need for countries in the region to exercise control over their exclusive economic zones, 200-mile swathes of continental shelf which may contain large deposits of oil, gas or other minerals.

Countries that have already beefed up their navies include Thailand, which recently took delivery of its first aircraft carrier. India is reported to be mulling a replacement for its aged aircraft carrier.
China is reported to have taken delivery of two Russian missile cruisers that will allow it to project power into the vital sea lanes of the South China Sea.
"Naval forces in the region are undergoing major expansion," Marriott said.
Increased naval spending is also being spurred by overlapping claims -- and angry rows -- to areas like the Spratly islands that are believed to hold rich deposits of oil and gas.
The dispute erupted anew when the Philippines protested at the presence of three Chinese naval warships in the area. Beijing denied the allegations.
The Spratlys are claimed in whole or in part by China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and the Philippines. Security experts say it may be the next hotspot in the region.

The Philippines, whose economy is just beginning to make some headway, has embarked on a programme to replace World War Two vintage ships with gunboats that could fire over-the-horizon missiles to repel threats to its 7,000 islands.
Defence experts said the naval show will give military officials in the Asia-Pacific region a chance to shop and look at the latest in naval technology for gunboats and guided missiles.
The warships docking here include the British aircraft carrier HMS Illustrious, while the Canadian navy will be represented by the HMCS Vancouver, a frigate, and the HMCS Huron, a destroyer.
